{{Short description|Non-empty convex set in Euclidean space}}
[[File:POV-Ray-Dodecahedron.svg|thumb|A [[dodecahedron]] is a convex body.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''convex body''' in <math>n</math>-[[dimension]]al [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> is a [[Compact space|compact]] [[convex set]] with non-[[Empty set|empty]] [[Interior (topology)|interior]]. Some authors do not require a non-empty interior, merely that the set is non-empty.

A convex body <math>K</math> is called '''symmetric''' if it is centrally symmetric with respect to the origin; that is to say, a point <math>x</math> lies in <math>K</math> [[if and only if]] its [[Antipodal point|antipode]], <math>- x</math> also lies in <math>K.</math> Symmetric convex bodies are in a [[Bijection|one-to-one correspondence]] with the [[unit ball]]s of [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]] on <math>\R^n.</math>

Some commonly known examples of convex bodies are the [[Euclidean ball]], the [[hypercube]] and the [[cross-polytope]].

== Metric space structure ==
Write <math>\mathcal K^n</math> for the set of convex bodies in <math>\mathbb R^n</math>. Then <math>\mathcal K^n</math> is a [[complete metric space]] with metric
<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Hug |first1=Daniel |last2=Weil |first2=Wolfgang|author2-link=Wolfgang Weil (mathematician) |date=2020 |title=Lectures on Convex Geometry |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-50180-8 |journal=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=286 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-50180-8 |isbn=978-3-030-50179-2 |issn=0072-5285|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
<math display="block">d(K,L) := \inf\{\epsilon \geq 0 : K \subset L + B^n(\epsilon), L \subset K + B^n(\epsilon) \}.</math>

Further, the [[Blaschke selection theorem|Blaschke Selection Theorem]] says that every ''d''-bounded sequence in <math>\mathcal K^n</math> has a convergent subsequence.<ref name=":0" />

==Polar body==
If <math>K</math> is a bounded convex body containing the origin <math>O</math> in its interior, the '''polar body''' <math>K^*</math> is <math>\{u : \langle u,v \rangle \leq 1, \forall v \in K \} </math>. The polar body has several nice properties including <math>(K^*)^*=K</math>, <math>K^*</math> is bounded, and if <math>K_1\subset K_2</math> then <math>K_2^*\subset K_1^*</math>. The polar body is a type of [[Duality (mathematics)|duality]] relation.
